处理器通过定位句柄移动它自己的文件订阅：驱动任务执行客户端的定位，从旧位置排入队列的内容被丢弃。

The parts of ruststream-sea-file a service on a stream file or a shell pipeline uses, one page per component.
With asyncapi each broker is a server and each FileStream channel carries its stream key in the x-ruststream-file extension.
A FileStream subscription and a file publish describe their channel with the stream key; bare keys and stdio describe nothing.
The file broker reports the path of its stream file and the stdio broker its protocol name; neither reports a host.
Two brokers and no server: FileBroker keeps a log in one .ss stream file, StdioBroker makes the process's pipes a stream.
beacon_interval sets how far apart the file's beacons sit; denser beacons seek in finer steps and make the file larger.
end_with_eos writes an end-of-stream mark at shutdown; a live subscription ends on it and a replay completes at it.
SeaFileError is the crate's one error type: connect, subscribe, receive, publish and seek failures, a closed broker, an invalid input.
existing_only makes startup fail when the stream file is missing, for a service that reads a file another process writes.
FileBroker::new records the path of a stream file; the runtime opens it at startup and creates it when it is missing.
loopback sends a stage's own output back to its input, so a stdio service runs in one process; it is a test aid.
Glob file::prelude on a stream file, stdio::prelude on a pipeline, and the crate prelude only in a service that uses both.
Shutdown flushes and closes the stream file; a publisher kept from before returns NotConnected, and a stdio shutdown ends every stdio stream.
size_limit caps the stream file at a size the operator chose; without it the file grows without limit.
StdioBroker reads standard input and writes standard output, so a service runs as one stage of a shell pipeline.
Headers travel inside the payload: a message with headers is written as rs1: or rs2: plus base64, one without is written as it is.
An envelope is the format a record carries headers in: Rs by default, Framed for a codec document per message, NoOp for the payload alone, or the service's own.
A pipe carries binary, multi-line and padded payloads intact: the stdio publisher envelopes any payload a text line would change.
Every delivery carries its sequence number in the stream-sequence header, from one on a stream file and from zero on a pipe.
FilePosition names a place in a stream key's log: the beginning, the tip, a sequence number, or an instant.
A batch body reaches the seek handle through FileBatchContext, which holds no position; each element carries its own sequence.
Ctx<Position> binds the delivery's place in the file; seeking back to it redelivers exactly that message.
Ctx<SeekHandle> moves the running subscription; what was queued is discarded and a position past the tip is refused.
start_at opens a subscription at a position on every startup; a stored sequence is how a service resumes on a stream file.
Publish is each form's one policy and its default: replies, slots and lifecycle hooks publish through it with no per-message setting.
A file publish appends under the destination's stream key and flushes, so a live subscriber or another reader sees it once the call returns.
A stdio publish writes one line to standard output under its stream key; an empty message is refused because a pipe drops empty lines.
ack and nack report Unsupported on both brokers: nothing records how far a service read, so it resumes from a stored position.
dead_letter names the stream key a spent delivery is written to, with its payload, its headers and its delivery count.
On a pipe a deferred copy goes to the next stage, so the mount site names it with out_retry(Publish).to(key) or the service does not start.
max_attempts caps how many deliveries a message gets, counted in the framework's retry-count header that every copy carries.
On a stream file a retry_after copy is appended under the key the subscription reads, so it comes back with nothing named at the mount site.
A stream key in #[subscriber] is a subscription on both brokers; on a stream file it follows the live tail of that key.
A slice handler takes a batch assembled on the client, up to the size batch(n) names; a partial batch leaves 10 ms after its first delivery.
FileStream names one stream key of the file and is the descriptor the generated document describes.
A stdio subscription reads the lines of its stream key; a line with no key in its header reaches every subscription.
replay reads the whole retained file once and completes at its end or at the end-of-stream mark, instead of following writes.

ruststream-sea-file 是 RustStream 的文件与 stdio 传输，基于 sea-streamer-file 和 sea-streamer-stdio 构建。它有两种传输。流文件是磁盘上单个 .ss 文件里的一份日志：它在重启后依然保留，订阅者可以重放它，或者回到更早的位置。标准输入和标准输出 则让服务成为 shell 管道里的一环。两者都不需要服务器。 这些指南带你把任一种传输上的服务从安装一路推进到生产环境。 从快速开始读起。

ruststream-sea-file 如何测量自己：三个循环、读取流文件的两种方式、受存储限制的判定计算，以及代码计数。流程就是框架自己的流程（RustStream 方法论），本页说明它在流文件上是什么样子。

一个进程把每个场景跑三遍，作为三个循环，它们只有一处不同：承载消息的是什么。 裸客户端。 直接驱动 sea-streamer-file：它的 streamer、消费者和生产者。 Broker crate。 本 crate，上面什么也没有：FileBroker 建立连接，FileStream 打开一个订阅，一个循环从它的流中取出投递、解码并结算。 RustStream。 用户写的服务：一个 #[subscriber] 处理器及其外围的应用。 其余一切在三个循环中都相同：流文件、消费者选项、解码成同一个结构体、载荷字节、带四个工作线程的 tokio 运行时，以及二进制程序。裸客户端没有结算要做，本 crate 的结算会立即报告 AckError::Unsupported，因此没有哪个循环需要等待结算。 消息体是 512 字节的 JSON。它解码成一个包含两个整数字段的结构体，因此解码不做内存分配，数字反映的是本 crate，而不是 JSON 解析器。
重放。 先写好整个文件，然后每个循环从开头读取它。文件比计时窗口统计的数量多出 8192 条消息体，因此没有哪个循环会读到末尾。 实时跟随。 先打开订阅，每个循环一边读取，一边通过自己的那一层追加。和本 crate 的发布者一样，每次追加都在下一次之前刷写到文件，写入者最多领先读取者 32 768 条消息。

每次运行使用新的流文件。 它位于 target/bench-streams 下，运行结束时删除，因此一次运行永远读不到之前的运行留下的东西。 在三个循环中，计时窗口都从第一次投递开始，到最后一个处理器返回时结束。 打开文件、创建消费者和写入被记录的区域都在窗口之外。 消息条数来自一次探测，它用 100 000 条消息测量裸循环的速率，因此在任何机器上，测量的运行都至少持续五秒。条数最多为两百万条消息，约合一 GiB 的流文件。 各循环交替进行：裸、crate、RustStream，共三轮。每个循环报告它最佳、中位和最差的一轮。 页缓存是热的。 每次运行都在读回文件之前刚刚写入它，因此这些数字反映的是文件系统，而不是设备。 当裸客户端在运行中一直在等待追加时，该行标为 受存储限制。这是算出来的：一次探测在 5000 次预热之后，为 50 000 次追加计时，每次追加都刷写到文件。实时跟随每次投递等待一次追加，重放则不等待。等待时间达到每条消息测得时间的一半时，该行就被标记。一次追加的时间与机器信息一起公布，因此这个计算可以核对。

开销图的每个场景都是用户写的服务，基于 FileBroker，使用自己的流文件，构建时不带 testing 特性。服务运行在单线程运行时上。服务启动之后，另一个线程通过客户端追加消息，这部分工作在测量区间之外。 指令数来自 callgrind，内存分配来自 DHAT。一个场景依次在一次投递、1000 次、2000 次上运行。后两次之差是一条消息的稳态开销，单次投递就是冷启动。 同一个二进制程序运行五次，每条消息的数字相差在千分之五以内。唯一的例外是应答的内存分配，它在 70 到 74 之间变动，取决于服务等待写入者的次数。一次运行的指令总数最多变动 2.7%。因此，与保存的基线对照时，某个场景的指令数多出百分之六就算失败。内存分配在每次运行中都受每个场景声明的下限约束。

just bench 这条命令让两个对照场景都经过全部三个循环，删除流文件，并重写 docs/benchmarks/results.json。它需要独占机器，并且会通过 target/bench-streams 写入数 GiB 的数据，每次一个文件，最大约一 GiB。它会清空 RUSTFLAGS，因此二进制程序不会绑定到构建它的 CPU 上。两条命令都按发布版本的方式构建基准测试，跨 crate 启用完整的链接时优化（fat LTO），因此这些数字描述的正是服务实际使用的代码。 just bench-code 代码计数大约需要一分钟，并且需要 valgrind；这条命令会自行安装基准测试运行器。just bench-code 5000 改为在五千次投递上测量，而不是一千次。在 main 上运行 just bench-code --save-baseline=main 记录基线，在分支上运行 just bench-code --baseline=main 与它对照。

ack、drop、retry 和 retry_after 在流文件和管道上变成什么。二者既不保存消费者的位置，也不确认任何东西。 处理器在流文件或管道上的结果：只有运行时发布的副本能把消息带回来处理器的结果ack、drop：报告不受支持，记录日志retry()：重新入队不受支持，记录日志retry_after(d)：运行时发布一份副本没有任何东西记录服务读到了哪里：重启后从它保存的位置继续 以文字阅读本图 处理器的结果 → ack、drop： 报告 不受支持， 记录日志 处理器的结果 → retry()： 重新入队 不受支持， 记录日志 处理器的结果 → retry_after(d)： 运行时 发布 一份副本 没有任何东西记录服务读到了哪里： 重启后从它保存的位置继续 两个客户端都不记录读取者处理过什么。因此，投递的 ack 和 nack 会立即报告 AckError::Unsupported，运行时记录日志。被确认的消息不会在任何地方留下标记，重新入队的消息也不会回来。重启的服务从它自己保存的位置继续。 重试是唯一能把消息带回来的结果，而且全部由运行时完成。

The parts of ruststream-sea-file a service uses, one page per component: the two brokers (FileBroker on a stream file and StdioBroker on a pipeline) and their settings, their subscriptions, positions and seeking, their publish policies, acknowledgement and retries, the headers a message carries, the AsyncAPI document, and the in-process transport a TestApp test runs on.

With the asyncapi feature each broker is a server of the generated document, and each FileStream channel carries its stream key in the x-ruststream-file extension. The core builds the AsyncAPI document from the app, before anything connects. This crate adds what it knows about the two transports. A server reports the path of the stream file, or the protocol name stdio. A channel on a stream file reports the stream key behind it. The specification lists no binding for a file transport or for stdio, and its protocol keys are a closed list. So the stream key travels in this crate's own extension, x-ruststream-file, which carries no binding version. Everything comes from the service's own declarations: the brokers, the descriptors and the destinations the mount sites resolved. The binary #[ruststream::app] writes prints the document with asyncapi gen.

The dependency line: ruststream-sea-file = { version = "0.7", features = ["asyncapi"] } The service registers its stream file under the label file and its pipeline under pipe, the keys of their servers in the document. cargo run --example sea_asyncapi --features asyncapi -- asyncapi gen prints the document. A FileStream subscription and a file publish describe their channel with the stream key; bare keys and stdio describe nothing. A subscription opened through FileStream reports the stream key it reads, as { "x-ruststream-file": { "streamKey": "orders" } } in the channel's bindings. A subscription opened by a bare stream key, #[subscriber("orders")], carries no descriptor, so its channel has no bindings. That is every stdio subscription, and a file subscription mounted without FileStream. A channel the service publishes to on a stream file carries the same extension, with the destination the mount site resolved: a reply's stream key, an Out slot's, the dead-letter one. One stream key is both ends of the file, so a channel reads the same whether the service reads it or appends to it. A stdio publish describes nothing, as a stdio subscription does. The path of the file stays on the server.

The channels orders and receipts carry their stream keys. The stdio channels lines and lines.out have no bindings. The file broker reports the path of its stream file and the stdio broker its protocol name; neither reports a host. A broker registered with with_broker_labeled is a server of the document, under its label. Both transports run inside the process, with nothing to connect to over a network, so a server has no host. The file broker's protocol is file, and its description is the path of the stream file, where a reader finds the log. The stdio broker's protocol is stdio, and it reports nothing else. Neither server carries a protocolVersion or bindings.

The stream file and the pipeline, registered under the labels file and pipe, come out as these two servers: "servers": { "file": { "protocol": "file", "description": "/var/lib/ruststream/orders.ss" }, "pipe": { "protocol": "stdio" } } Macros Manual examples/sea_asyncapi.rs /// The stream file the service records orders in. fn file_broker() -> FileBroker { FileBroker::new("/var/lib/ruststream/orders.ss") } /// The pipeline the service is a stage of. fn stdio_broker() -> StdioBroker { StdioBroker::new() } examples/manual/sea_asyncapi.rs /// The stream file the service records orders in. fn file_broker() -> FileBroker { FileBroker::new("/var/lib/ruststream/orders.ss") } /// The pipeline the service is a stage of. fn stdio_broker() -> StdioBroker { StdioBroker::new() }

Two brokers and no server: FileBroker keeps a log in one .ss stream file, and StdioBroker makes the process's standard input and output a stream. A stream file is a log on disk. It keeps what was written across restarts, and a subscriber can replay it or move back to an earlier message. A stdio service is one stage of a shell pipeline: it reads lines on standard input and writes lines on standard output. Neither transport has a host to connect to, so nothing is installed and nothing listens. Inside one transport, messages are grouped by stream key, a name such as orders. A stream key in #[subscriber("orders")] is a subscription on both brokers. A publish names the stream key it goes to. Both brokers follow the same lifecycle. new only records the configuration and does no I/O, so the whole service fits the synchronous #[ruststream::app] builder. At startup the runtime connects the broker: the stream file is opened, or the process's pipes are attached. Every subscription and every publisher of the service opens against that connected form, ConnectedFileBroker or ConnectedStdioBroker. At shutdown the runtime closes it. A service on one transport imports that transport's prelude. A failure of either broker is a SeaFileError.

The service reads the stream key orders of the file /var/lib/orders/orders.ss from its start. cargo run --example file_service --features testing -- run starts it, and creates the file when it is missing. beacon_interval sets how far apart the file's beacons sit; denser beacons seek in finer steps and make the file larger. A beacon is an index entry the file client writes into the stream file at a fixed interval of bytes. Beacons are the file's index: a seek finds its place in the file by them, so closer beacons make seeking finer-grained. Each beacon takes room in the file. The client's default is one beacon every 1 MiB. The interval is a number of bytes, a positive multiple of 1024. Any other value fails startup with SeaFileError::Invalid, in a TestApp test as on a real file. The interval is written into the header of a file the broker creates.

The broker writes a beacon every 64 KiB. The test reads the interval back out of the header of the file it created. Macros Manual examples/file_broker_beacons.rs /// A beacon every 64 KiB of the file: sixteen times as dense as the client's default of 1 MiB. fn broker(path: &str) -> FileBroker { FileBroker::new(path).beacon_interval(64 * 1024) } fn service(path: &str) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker(path), |b| { b.include(handle); }) } examples/manual/file_broker_beacons.rs /// A beacon every 64 KiB of the file: sixteen times as dense as the client's default of 1 MiB. fn broker(path: &str) -> FileBroker { FileBroker::new(path).beacon_interval(64 * 1024) } fn service(path: &str) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker(path), |b| { b.include(subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Accept).build()); }) }

end_with_eos writes an end-of-stream mark at shutdown; a live subscription ends on it and a replay completes at it. A live subscription follows the file and waits for the next write. The mark is the one thing that ends it: a subscription that reads up to the mark delivers every message before it and then ends. A replay reads the file once and completes at the mark, or at the end of the file when there is none. A subscription that opens at the tip of a finished file starts after the mark, so it reads what is appended later. The mark is how a recorder tells its readers that a log is complete. After it, a seek on a live subscription is refused.

The recorder marks its file finished when it shuts down. In the test an auditor reads the receipts from the start of that file, ends at the mark, and never reads a receipt appended after it. Macros Manual examples/file_broker_eos.rs /// The recorder: when it shuts down, the file is marked finished. fn writer(path: &str) -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = FileBroker::new(path).end_with_eos(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("recorder", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(record); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { writer("/var/lib/orders/orders.ss") } examples/manual/file_broker_eos.rs /// The recorder: when it shuts down, the file is marked finished. fn writer(path: &str) -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = FileBroker::new(path).end_with_eos(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("recorder", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Record) .reply() .build(), ); }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { writer("/var/lib/orders/orders.ss") }

SeaFileError is the crate's one error type: connect, subscribe, receive, publish and seek failures, a closed broker, an invalid input. Each variant names the step that failed, with the file path or the stream key it failed on. The client's own error is its source, so the client's types stay out of the crate's API. Variant When Connect the stream file could not be opened or created, or standard input and output could not be attached Subscribe a subscription could not be opened Receive an open subscription failed to read Publish the client refused to write a message Seek a subscription could not be moved to a position NotConnected a publisher was used after its broker shut down Invalid a stream key the client does not take, an empty message on standard output, or a beacon interval that is not a multiple of 1024 A service meets the error in two places. A failed startup carries it as the source of the runtime's error, and the service exits before it reads anything. A publish from a handler returns it inside the core's PublishError, and the handler decides what to do with the delivery. The enum is #[non_exhaustive], so a match on it ends with a wildcard arm.

The stage writes each job's note to standard output as its bytes. A pipe drops an empty line, so an empty note is refused with Invalid; the handler logs the error and finishes the job without the note. Macros Manual examples/sea_broker_errors.rs #[subscriber("jobs")] async fn annotate(job: &Job, Out(notes): Out<impl Publisher, Notes>) -> HandlerOutcome { let note = Note(job.note.clone().into_bytes()); if let Err(err) = notes.message(&note).publish().await { // An empty note is refused, and the job is done without it. tracing::warn!(subscription = "jobs", job.id, error = %err, "note not written"); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sea_broker_errors.rs struct Annotate; impl<Entry> Handle<Job, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Annotate where Entry: OutEntry<Notes, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, job: &Job, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let note = Note(job.note.clone().into_bytes()); if let Err(err) = outs.get(Notes).message(&note).publish().await { // An empty note is refused, and the job is done without it. tracing::warn!(subscription = "jobs", job.id, error = %err, "note not written"); } Ok(()) } }

existing_only makes startup fail when the stream file is missing, for a service that reads a file another process writes. Without the setting, startup creates a missing file and the service reads an empty log. For a reader that is the wrong answer: a mistyped path, or a writer that has not run yet, leaves it with nothing to read and no error. With the setting, startup fails with SeaFileError::Connect, which names the path, and no file is created. A file that is there opens as usual. In a TestApp test the stream file is a log in memory, and it counts as the file the operator provisioned. So the refusal shows only against a real file, with TestApp::start_live.

The auditor reads the orders the order service writes to its file. The test starts the auditor on a missing path, and startup fails; once the order service has created the file, the auditor starts and reads it. Macros Manual examples/file_broker_existing_only.rs /// A reader of the file the order service writes: it never creates the file itself. fn reader(path: &str) -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = FileBroker::new(path).existing_only(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("auditor", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(audit); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { reader("/var/lib/orders/orders.ss") } examples/manual/file_broker_existing_only.rs /// A reader of the file the order service writes: it never creates the file itself. fn reader(path: &str) -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = FileBroker::new(path).existing_only(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("auditor", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Audit).build()); }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { reader("/var/lib/orders/orders.ss") }

FileBroker::new records the path of a stream file; the runtime opens it at startup and creates it when it is missing. A stream file holds one log per stream key, in the .ss format of sea-streamer-file. Each stream key is numbered from one, and the numbering carries on when a later run appends to the same file. A service that reads a file another service writes requires it with existing_only instead. A publish appends the message under its stream key and flushes it, so the bytes reach the operating system before the call returns. The file is synced to the device when the broker shuts down. The file grows without limit, unless size_limit caps it. The file client builds on Unix systems only, so the file transport does not build on Windows. Two more settings shape the file itself: end_with_eos marks it finished at shutdown, and beacon_interval sets how densely it is indexed.

The service confirms each order on the stream key receipts of the same file. The test starts it on a path where no file exists yet, and the file is there once startup returns. Macros Manual examples/file_broker.rs /// The service on the stream file at `path`. fn service(path: &str) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(FileBroker::new(path), |b| { b.include(confirm); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service("/var/lib/orders/orders.ss") } examples/manual/file_broker.rs /// The service on the stream file at `path`. fn service(path: &str) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(FileBroker::new(path), |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Confirm) .reply() .build(), ); }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service("/var/lib/orders/orders.ss") }

loopback sends a stage's own output back to its input, so a stdio service runs in one process; it is a test aid. Without it, a line the service writes reaches the next process of the pipeline, and the service's own subscriptions never read it. With it, the line also reaches every subscription of the service on the same stream key. So two stages of a pipeline run in one process, and a test drives both without a shell. A subscription under loopback reads the service's output as well as standard input, so the end of standard input leaves it open until shutdown. In a TestApp test the pipe is held in memory and follows the same rule: the service reads its own output only under loopback. Without it, a test reads what the service wrote with published::<T>(key). A service ships without loopback: a stage that works only under it stops working in a real pipeline.

The counting stage and the totalling stage run in one process. The count the first one writes under counts comes back to the second. Macros Manual examples/stdio_broker_loopback.rs /// Both stages in one process, as a test runs them. #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { let broker = StdioBroker::new().loopback(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("word-count", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(count).out_retry(Publish).to("lines.retry"); b.include(total).out_retry(Publish).to("counts.retry"); }) } examples/manual/stdio_broker_loopback.rs /// Both stages in one process, as a test runs them. fn app() -> impl App { let broker = StdioBroker::new().loopback(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("word-count", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber("lines", Count).reply().build()) .out_retry(Publish) .to("lines.retry"); b.include(subscriber("counts", Total).build()) .out_retry(Publish) .to("counts.retry"); }) }

Glob file::prelude on a stream file, stdio::prelude on a pipeline, and the crate prelude only in a service that uses both. Each glob carries the core's own prelude, so #[subscriber], RustStream, HandlerOutcome and Out come with it. use ruststream_sea_file::file::prelude::*; adds FileBroker, the descriptor FileStream, the positions FilePosition, the context keys Position and SeekHandle, and the publish policy as Publish. use ruststream_sea_file::stdio::prelude::*; adds StdioBroker and its policy as Publish. Publish is the name every broker crate gives its publish policy, so a mount site reads the same on every transport. Moving a service from one transport to the other changes the glob and the broker, and leaves the mount sites alone. The two transports would claim the same name Publish, so the crate prelude carries neither. A service on both brokers globs it and writes the prefixed FilePublish and StdioPublish.

One service records orders from a stream file and answers orders read on standard input. Macros Manual examples/sea_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_sea_file::prelude::*; #[subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), reply("receipts"))] async fn record(order: &Order) -> Receipt { Receipt { order: order.id } } #[subscriber("orders", reply("receipts"))] async fn answer(order: &Order) -> Receipt { Receipt { order: order.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(FileBroker::new("/var/lib/orders/orders.ss"), |b| { b.include(record).out_reply(FilePublish); }) .with_broker(StdioBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(answer) .out_reply(StdioPublish) .out_retry(StdioPublish) .to("orders.retry"); }) } examples/manual/sea_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_sea_file::prelude::*; struct Record; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for Record { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Receipt { order: order.id })) } } struct Answer; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for Answer { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Receipt { order: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(FileBroker::new("/var/lib/orders/orders.ss"), |b| { let record = subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Record); b.include(record.reply().to("receipts").build()) .out_reply(FilePublish); }) .with_broker(StdioBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Answer).reply().to("receipts").build()) .out_reply(StdioPublish) .out_retry(StdioPublish) .to("orders.retry"); }) }

Shutdown flushes and closes the stream file; a publisher kept from before returns SeaFileError::NotConnected, and a stdio shutdown ends every stdio stream of the process. The file broker's shutdown waits for the publishes in flight, then ends the file's writer. The writer writes the end-of-stream mark when the broker asks for one, and syncs the file to the device. When shutdown returns, the file is closed, so an after_shutdown hook of the app can move, copy or remove it. Brokers opened on one path in one process share the file's writer: the first of them to shut down ends it, and a publish through the others fails. A publisher taken before the shutdown, such as the one a startup hook received, still points at the closed broker. A publish through it returns NotConnected and never succeeds against the closed file. The stdio transport belongs to the whole process. Shutting a StdioBroker down ends every stdio subscription and publisher in the process, not only the ones that broker opened. Each subscription first delivers the lines it has already read, then ends.

Once the broker has closed the file, the app's after_shutdown hook moves it aside, and the next run starts a new one. The test runs the hook's function after the harness shut the broker down, and the moved file opens as a whole stream file. Macros Manual examples/sea_broker_shutdown.rs /// Moves the finished stream file aside, so the next run starts a new one. fn archive(path: &str) -> io::Result<()> { fs::rename(path, format!("{path}.done")) } fn service(path: &str) -> impl App<State = ()> { let finished = path.to_owned(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Runs after the broker has shut down: the file is synced and closed. .after_shutdown(async move |_state| archive(&finished)) .with_broker(FileBroker::new(path), |b| { b.include(record); }) } examples/manual/sea_broker_shutdown.rs /// Moves the finished stream file aside, so the next run starts a new one. fn archive(path: &str) -> io::Result<()> { fs::rename(path, format!("{path}.done")) } fn service(path: &str) -> impl App<State = ()> { let finished = path.to_owned(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Runs after the broker has shut down: the file is synced and closed. .after_shutdown(async move |_state| archive(&finished)) .with_broker(FileBroker::new(path), |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Record) .reply() .build(), ); }) }

size_limit caps the stream file at a size the operator chose; without it the file grows without limit. The cap counts every byte of the file, the bytes an earlier run wrote included. The publish that reaches the cap fails with SeaFileError::Publish, and every later publish to that file returns that error at once. Publishes in flight at that moment each return, and each one reported done is in the file whole. At the cap the file client behaves in two ways a reader of the file notices. A message that fills the cap exactly is written whole, and its publish still fails: a reader of the file reads a message whose publish reported an error. A message larger than the space left is cut at the cap, and a reader stops before it. A file already larger than the cap fails startup with SeaFileError::Invalid, which names the size and the cap. Brokers opened on one path in one process share the file's writer, and with it the cap of the first one to connect. In a TestApp test the stream file is a log in memory, and it counts each message in the bytes the file client writes for it, beacons included. So the cap falls on the same message as on a real file, with the same three outcomes. A message larger than the space left is refused whole in memory, where a real file holds its first bytes; a reader sees it in neither. A message the test itself injects past the cap ends the test with a panic, because an injection has no error to return.

The recorder's log may take 64 GiB of the disk. The tests cap a file at 1 KiB and publish until a publish fails, and start the recorder on a file an earlier run left larger than its cap. Macros Manual examples/file_broker_size_limit.rs /// A recorder whose log may take `limit` bytes of the disk and no more. fn recorder(path: &str, limit: NonZeroU64) -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = FileBroker::new(path).size_limit(limit); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("recorder", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(record); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { recorder("/var/lib/readings/readings.ss", nonzero!(64 << 30)) } examples/manual/file_broker_size_limit.rs /// A recorder whose log may take `limit` bytes of the disk and no more. fn recorder(path: &str, limit: NonZeroU64) -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = FileBroker::new(path).size_limit(limit); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("recorder", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber(FileStream::new("readings"), Record).build()); }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { recorder("/var/lib/readings/readings.ss", nonzero!(64 << 30)) }

StdioBroker reads standard input and writes standard output, so a service runs as one stage of a shell pipeline. StdioBroker::new takes no settings. At startup the runtime attaches the process's own standard input and output, over sea-streamer-stdio. Standard input is where every subscription reads, and standard output is where every publish writes. So producer | service | consumer connects three processes with nothing in between. Each line is one message in the client's format, [timestamp | stream_key | sequence | shard_id] payload, with every field in the brackets optional. The stream key is part of the line, so one stage reads several keys from one input. A subscription reads the lines of its own stream key. A line the service writes goes to the next process, never back to this one. So a delayed retry has no address on this transport, and every registration names where its deferred copies go with .out_retry(Publish).to(key). A registration that names none fails startup, and the error names the subscription. loopback sends the output back to the input, for tests that run several stages in one process. When standard input ends, every subscription ends after the lines it has already read. The guide Shell pipelines shows a stage that then shuts down and exits. The transport belongs to the whole process. Shutting the broker down ends every stdio subscription and publisher in the process. The guide Shell pipelines feeds a stage, reads its output and chains stages.

The stage reads text under lines and writes a word count under counts. echo '[2024-01-01T00:00:00 | lines | 1] {"body":"one two three"}' \ | cargo run --example stdio_broker --features testing -- run Macros Manual examples/stdio_broker.rs use ruststream_sea_file::stdio::prelude::*; #[subscriber("lines", reply)] async fn count(text: &Text) -> Counted { Counted { words: text.body.split_whitespace().count(), } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("word-count", "0.1.0")).with_broker(StdioBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(count).out_retry(Publish).to("lines.retry"); }) } examples/manual/stdio_broker.rs use ruststream_sea_file::stdio::prelude::*; struct Count; impl Handle<Text, Counted> for Count { fn handle( &self, text: &Text, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Counted, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Counted { words: text.body.split_whitespace().count(), })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("word-count", "0.1.0")).with_broker(StdioBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("lines", Count).reply().build()) .out_retry(Publish) .to("lines.retry"); }) }

Headers travel inside the payload: a message with headers is written as rs1: or rs2: plus base64, one without is written as it is. A stream file entry and a line on a pipe carry a stream key and a payload, with no room for headers. So a message with headers is written as an envelope: a prefix, then base64 of a header block followed by the payload. The prefix rs1: marks a block of name: value lines. It is used whenever every header reads back unchanged from a line, which keeps the message readable by earlier releases of this crate. The prefix rs2: marks a block where each name and value is length-prefixed. It is used when a value is not UTF-8, holds a line break, or begins or ends with whitespace, so a value travels byte for byte. The envelope is text, so it fits on a line of a pipe. A message with no headers is written as it is, so a file recorded that way stays readable by any sea-streamer consumer, and a file another tool wrote is readable here. A payload that itself begins with rs1: or rs2: is enveloped, so no reader takes it for an envelope. This is the default envelope; a broker, a subscription or a publish policy can choose another on Envelopes. A handler reads headers with Headers<T> or ctx.headers() as on any broker, and the delivery parses them the first time they are read. Every delivery also carries its position in SEQUENCE_HEADER.

The service confirms each order under the tenant header it arrived with, and the receipt carries the same header. Macros Manual examples/sea_headers.rs /// The header contract every order and receipt carries. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize)] struct Tenant { tenant: String, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders", headers = Tenant)] struct Order { id: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts", headers = Tenant)] struct Receipt { order: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Receipt)] struct Receipts; /// Confirms an order under the tenant it arrived with. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"))] async fn confirm( order: &Order, Headers(tenant): Headers<Tenant>, Out(receipts): Out<impl Publisher, Receipts>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, tenant = %tenant.tenant, "confirmed"); let receipt = Receipt { order: order.id }; if receipts .message(&receipt) .with_headers(&tenant) .publish() .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The service on the file `main` hands it. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("checkout", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include(confirm).out(Receipts, Publish).build(); }) } examples/manual/sea_headers.rs /// The header contract every order and receipt carries. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Tenant { tenant: String, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "orders", headers = Tenant)] struct Order { id: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "receipts", headers = Tenant)] struct Receipt { order: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Receipt)] struct Receipts; /// Confirms an order under the tenant it arrived with. struct Confirm; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Confirm where Entry: OutEntry<Receipts, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let Headers(tenant) = Headers::<Tenant>::from_context(ctx).await?; tracing::info!(order.id, tenant = %tenant.tenant, "confirmed"); let receipt = Receipt { order: order.id }; if outs .get(Receipts) .message(&receipt) .with_headers(&tenant) .publish() .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } /// The service on the file `main` hands it. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("checkout", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include(subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Confirm).build()) .out(Receipts, Publish) .build(); }) }

An envelope is the format a record carries headers in: Rs by default, Framed for a codec document per message, NoOp for the payload alone, or the service's own. The envelope is chosen like a codec, and the most specific level wins. The broker sets the default with FileBroker::new(path).envelope(..) or StdioBroker::new().envelope(..). A subscription on a stream file reads in its own with b.include(handler.envelope(NoOp)), or FileStream::new(key).envelope(..) on the manual path, and a publish policy writes in its own with Publish.envelope(..). The step composes with a start position in either order: the attribute's start_at(..), or the mount-site .start_at(..) before or after it. The choice is a type, so it costs nothing per message. Rs writes a message with headers as rs1: or rs2: plus base64, and a message without them as it is. This is the format of every earlier release, described on Envelope. Framed::new(codec) writes every message as one document of the codec: headers and exactly one payload field. The payload follows the convention of the CloudEvents formats. With JsonCodec, a payload that is a JSON text is embedded as a value in payload, byte for byte, and any other payload is base64 in payload_base64; on a pipe each line is a JSON object any line tool reads. A pipe line cannot hold a raw line break, so there a JSON payload with one travels as payload_base64. With CborCodec, MsgpackCodec or a codec of the service, which implements FrameCodec with an empty body, the payload is a byte string in payload. Header values are text in every document, and a header whose value is not UTF-8 fails the publish, naming the header and the destination. NoOp writes the payload as it is, and a delivery carries no envelope headers, only the transport's own stream-sequence. A publish that carries a header fails and names the header and the destination, and so does a payload a line on a pipe cannot carry. A record that is not in the subscription's envelope reads as a payload with no headers. A delivery parses its headers the first time something reads them, so a handler that reads only the payload never parses the envelope. A test addresses a broker by the type its envelope gives it, tb.broker::<FileBroker<NoOp>>(); a broker with an envelope of the service's own is registered once with ruststream::register_testable_broker!. The two JSON forms of a document are {"headers":{"event":"created"},"payload":{"id":7}} and {"headers":{"event":"created"},"payload_base64":"CAc="}. A document is recognised only in this exact shape; a record with both payload fields or with any other field reads as a foreign record. A recognised record whose header block does not parse reads as its payload with no headers, and the delivery logs it with the subscription and the envelope. The generated AsyncAPI document reports the media type of Framed records beside the channel.

The plant service reads the bare records a sensor gateway writes and sends its alerts as JSON documents, while the stream file keeps the default envelope. Macros Manual examples/sea_envelopes.rs /// A reading as the sensor gateway writes it: a bare JSON payload, no headers. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] struct Reading { sensor: String, millivolts: u32, } /// An alert the dashboard reads as JSON lines, with the plant in a header. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "alerts", headers = Plant)] struct Alert { sensor: String, } /// The header contract of an alert. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize)] struct Plant { plant: String, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Alert)] struct Alerts; /// Reads the gateway's bare records and raises an alert on a low reading. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("readings"))] async fn watch(reading: &Reading, Out(alerts): Out<impl Publisher, Alerts>) -> HandlerOutcome { if reading.millivolts >= 3000 { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } let alert = Alert { sensor: reading.sensor.clone(), }; let plant = Plant { plant: "north".to_owned(), }; if alerts .message(&alert) .with_headers(&plant) .publish() .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/sea_envelopes.rs /// The plant service: the stream file keeps the default envelope, the readings subscription reads /// bare records, the alerts go out as JSON documents, and the pipe reads the tab feed. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("plant", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(file, |b| { b.include(watch.envelope(NoOp)) .out(Alerts, FilePublish.envelope(Framed::new(JsonCodec))) .build(); }) .with_broker(StdioBroker::new().envelope(PlantTab), |b| { b.include(tally) .out_retry(StdioPublish) .to("readings.retry"); }) } examples/manual/sea_envelopes.rs /// A reading as the sensor gateway writes it: a bare JSON payload, no headers. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Reading { sensor: String, millivolts: u32, } /// An alert the dashboard reads as JSON lines, with the plant in a header. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "alerts", headers = Plant)] struct Alert { sensor: String, } /// The header contract of an alert. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Plant { plant: String, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Alert)] struct Alerts; /// Reads the gateway's bare records and raises an alert on a low reading. struct Watch; impl<Entry> Handle<Reading, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Watch where Entry: OutEntry<Alerts, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, reading: &Reading, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if reading.millivolts >= 3000 { return Ok(()); } let alert = Alert { sensor: reading.sensor.clone(), }; let plant = Plant { plant: "north".to_owned(), }; if outs .get(Alerts) .message(&alert) .with_headers(&plant) .publish() .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } examples/manual/sea_envelopes.rs /// The plant service: the stream file keeps the default envelope, the readings subscription reads /// bare records, the alerts go out as JSON documents, and the pipe reads the tab feed. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("plant", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(file, |b| { b.include(subscriber(FileStream::new("readings").envelope(NoOp), Watch).build()) .out(Alerts, FilePublish.envelope(Framed::new(JsonCodec))) .build(); }) .with_broker(StdioBroker::new().envelope(PlantTab), |b| { b.include(subscriber("readings", Tally).build()) .out_retry(StdioPublish) .to("readings.retry"); }) }

The pipe of the same service carries a feed whose lines hold the plant, a tab, and the payload. The envelope finds the payload behind the tab and parses the plant only when the handler reads it. Macros Manual examples/sea_envelopes.rs /// A feed whose lines hold the plant, a tab, and the payload. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, Default)] struct PlantTab; impl Envelope for PlantTab { /// Where the tab is, when the line has one. type Opened = Option<usize>; fn seal<'p>( &self, headers: &HeaderMap, payload: &'p [u8], _medium: Medium, ) -> Result<Cow<'p, [u8]>, SealError> { let plant = headers.get("plant").unwrap_or_default(); Ok(Cow::Owned([plant, b"\t", payload].concat())) } fn open(&self, record: &[u8]) -> Option<usize> { record.iter().position(|byte| *byte == b'\t') } fn payload<'r>(&self, record: &'r [u8], tab: &'r Option<usize>) -> &'r [u8] { tab.map_or(record, |tab| &record[tab + 1..]) } fn headers(&self, record: &[u8], tab: &Option<usize>) -> Option<HeaderMap> { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); if let Some(tab) = *tab { headers.insert( "plant", String::from_utf8_lossy(&record[..tab]).into_owned(), ); } Some(headers) } } /// Counts the readings of each plant that arrive on standard input. #[subscriber("readings")] async fn tally(reading: &Reading, Headers(plant): Headers<Plant>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(plant = %plant.plant, sensor = %reading.sensor, "counted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sea_envelopes.rs /// A feed whose lines hold the plant, a tab, and the payload. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, Default)] struct PlantTab; impl Envelope for PlantTab { /// Where the tab is, when the line has one. type Opened = Option<usize>; fn seal<'p>( &self, headers: &HeaderMap, payload: &'p [u8], _medium: Medium, ) -> Result<Cow<'p, [u8]>, SealError> { let plant = headers.get("plant").unwrap_or_default(); Ok(Cow::Owned([plant, b"\t", payload].concat())) } fn open(&self, record: &[u8]) -> Option<usize> { record.iter().position(|byte| *byte == b'\t') } fn payload<'r>(&self, record: &'r [u8], tab: &'r Option<usize>) -> &'r [u8] { tab.map_or(record, |tab| &record[tab + 1..]) } fn headers(&self, record: &[u8], tab: &Option<usize>) -> Option<HeaderMap> { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); if let Some(tab) = *tab { headers.insert( "plant", String::from_utf8_lossy(&record[..tab]).into_owned(), ); } Some(headers) } } /// Counts the readings of each plant that arrive on standard input. struct Tally; impl Handle<Reading> for Tally { async fn handle( &self, reading: &Reading, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let Headers(plant) = Headers::<Plant>::from_context(ctx).await?; tracing::info!(plant = %plant.plant, sensor = %reading.sensor, "counted"); Ok(()) } }
documents.s: An envelope of the service's own

documents.t: A pipe carries binary, multi-line and padded payloads intact: the stdio publisher envelopes any payload a text line would change. A line on a pipe is UTF-8 text: the reader splits its input at newlines and trims the space around each payload. So the default envelope of the stdio publisher envelopes a payload with no headers in four cases: it is not UTF-8, it holds a newline, it begins or ends with whitespace, or it begins with rs1: or rs2:. Any other payload leaves as it is, so a plain JSON message stays a readable line. The next stage opens the envelope and hands its handler the bytes that were published. A stream file holds bytes, so the file publisher envelopes only a message with headers and a payload that begins with rs1: or rs2:. A handler that keeps bytes as they are takes a Deserialized input and answers with a Serialized type, so no codec touches them.

The stage keeps the first kilobyte of each binary image as its thumbnail, for the next stage. Macros Manual examples/stdio_payloads.rs /// An image as it arrives, bytes the codec does not touch. #[derive(Deserialized)] struct Image<'a>(&'a [u8]); /// The bytes this stage hands the next one. #[derive(Outgoing, Serialized)] #[outgoing(name = "thumbnails")] struct Thumbnail(Vec<u8>); /// Keeps the first kilobyte of each image as its thumbnail. #[subscriber("images", reply)] async fn thumbnail(image: &Image<'_>) -> Thumbnail { let kept = image.0.len().min(1024); tracing::info!(bytes = image.0.len(), kept, "thumbnail"); Thumbnail(image.0[..kept].to_vec()) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("thumbnails", "0.1.0")).with_broker(StdioBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(thumbnail).out_retry(Publish).to("images.retry"); }) } examples/manual/stdio_payloads.rs /// An image as it arrives, bytes the codec does not touch. #[derive(Deserialized)] struct Image<'a>(&'a [u8]); /// The bytes this stage hands the next one. #[derive(Outgoing, Serialized)] #[outgoing(name = "thumbnails")] struct Thumbnail(Vec<u8>); /// Keeps the first kilobyte of each image as its thumbnail. struct Shrink; impl<'p> Handle<Image<'p>, Thumbnail> for Shrink { fn handle( &self, image: &Image<'p>, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Thumbnail, HandlerOutcome>> { let kept = image.0.len().min(1024); tracing::info!(bytes = image.0.len(), kept, "thumbnail"); ready(Ok(Thumbnail(image.0[..kept].to_vec()))) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("thumbnails", "0.1.0")).with_broker(StdioBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("images", Shrink).reply().build()) .out_retry(Publish) .to("images.retry"); }) }

Every delivery carries its sequence number in the stream-sequence header, from one on a stream file and from zero on a pipe. SEQUENCE_HEADER is the header's name, stream-sequence. The value is the number in decimal, as each client counts. A stream file numbers each stream key from one and keeps counting across restarts, so the number names the message's place in the file. A pipe numbers the lines of each key from zero, unless a line's header names a sequence of its own. The reader adds the header to every delivery, so the handler reads it with ctx.headers() like any other header. On a stream file Ctx<Position> gives the same place as a FilePosition, the form start_at and a seek take.

The service numbers each order with the sequence it sits at in the file. Macros Manual examples/file_sequence_header.rs /// Numbers each order with the sequence it sits at in the file. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), reply)] async fn number(order: &Order, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Result<Numbered, HandlerOutcome> { let Some(sequence) = ctx .headers() .get_str(SEQUENCE_HEADER) .and_then(|sequence| sequence.parse().ok()) else { return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); }; tracing::info!(order.id, sequence, "numbered"); Ok(Numbered { order: order.id, sequence, }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("numbering", "0.1.0")).with_broker( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss"), |b| { b.include(number); }, ) } examples/manual/file_sequence_header.rs /// Numbers each order with the sequence it sits at in the file. struct Number; impl Handle<Order, Numbered> for Number { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Numbered, HandlerOutcome>> { let Some(sequence) = ctx .headers() .get_str(SEQUENCE_HEADER) .and_then(|sequence| sequence.parse().ok()) else { return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); }; tracing::info!(order.id, sequence, "numbered"); ready(Ok(Numbered { order: order.id, sequence, })) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("numbering", "0.1.0")).with_broker( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss"), |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Number) .reply() .build(), ); }, ) }

FilePosition names a place in a stream key's log: the beginning, the tip, a sequence number, or an instant. A stream file keeps its log, so a subscription opens at a place in it with start_at, and a handler moves it with a seek. FilePosition::beginning() is the first message the file retains under the key. FilePosition::end() is the tip, where the next append lands. FilePosition::sequence(n) is message number n of the key, and the message itself is delivered again. A stream key is numbered from one, and the numbering carries on when a later run appends to the same file. FilePosition::timestamp(millis) is the first message stamped strictly later than that instant, in milliseconds since the Unix epoch. A delivery reports its own place as a sequence, which Ctx<Position> binds. The sequence the file writes next, one after its last message, is the tip. A sequence further ahead, and an instant later than every message the file holds, are refused. A position read off a delivery, the beginning and the tip are always within the file.

The revenue report is rebuilt from the first order the file retains on every startup, then follows the orders appended after. Macros Manual examples/file_position.rs /// Rebuilds the revenue report from the first order the file retains, then follows new orders. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), start_at(FilePosition::beginning()))] async fn report(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, order.total_cents, "counted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The report on the shop's stream file `main` hands it. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("revenue", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include(report); }) } examples/manual/file_position.rs /// Rebuilds the revenue report from the first order the file retains, then follows new orders. struct Report; impl Handle<Order> for Report { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, order.total_cents, "counted"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The report on the shop's stream file `main` hands it. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("revenue", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Report) .start_at(FilePosition::beginning()) .build(), ); }) }

A batch body reaches the seek handle through FileBatchContext, which holds no position; each element carries its own sequence. A batch spans many deliveries, so it has no single place in the file. The batch context holds what every delivery of the batch shares: the subscription's SeekHandle. A batch body takes ctx: &mut Context<'_, FileBatchContext> and reads the handle with ctx.context(SeekHandle). The batch settles first, so a seek from its body applies to the batches after it. The deliveries the current batch already holds stay in it. Each element's own sequence is in its stream-sequence header (SEQUENCE_HEADER). Position is a key of the per-delivery FileContext, which a single-message handler reads. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T], (), (), FileBatchContext>.

Job 1 says the jobs up to sequence 5 cannot be processed: the first batch holds jobs 1 to 3, and the next one opens at job 5. Macros Manual examples/file_batch_seek.rs /// A batch spans many deliveries, so its context is the subscription's: the seek handle, and no /// position. The move applies to the batches after this one. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("jobs"), start_at(FilePosition::beginning()))] async fn drain(jobs: &[Job], ctx: &mut Context<'_, FileBatchContext>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(jobs = jobs.len(), "drained"); let Some(resume_at) = jobs.iter().find_map(|job| job.resume_at) else { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); }; if let Err(error) = ctx .context(SeekHandle) .seek(FilePosition::sequence(resume_at)) .await { tracing::warn!(resume_at, %error, "seek refused"); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The worker on the job file `main` hands it, three jobs at a time. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include(drain.batch(nonzero!(3))); }) } examples/manual/file_batch_seek.rs /// A batch spans many deliveries, so its context is the subscription's: the seek handle, and no /// position. The move applies to the batches after this one. struct Drain; impl Handle<[Job], (), (), FileBatchContext> for Drain { async fn handle( &self, jobs: &[Job], _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, FileBatchContext>, ) -> Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(jobs = jobs.len(), "drained"); let Some(resume_at) = jobs.iter().find_map(|job| job.resume_at) else { return Ok(()); }; if let Err(error) = ctx .context(SeekHandle) .seek(FilePosition::sequence(resume_at)) .await { tracing::warn!(resume_at, %error, "seek refused"); } Ok(()) } } /// The worker on the job file `main` hands it, three jobs at a time. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("jobs"), Drain) .batch(nonzero!(3)) .start_at(FilePosition::beginning()) .build(), ); }) }

Ctx<Position> binds the delivery's place in the file; seeking back to it redelivers exactly that message. Position is a context key of the stream file form. Ctx(at): Ctx<Position> binds a FilePosition, and for a delivery it is always FilePosition::Sequence(n): the message's number under its key, counted from one. The value is pinned: a seek to it delivers that same message again, then the rest of the log in order. Stored, it is the checkpoint a later run hands to start_at. The same number travels in the delivery's stream-sequence header (SEQUENCE_HEADER), which each element of a batch carries too. In the manual form the body names FileContext as its context, impl Handle<Order, Reply, (), FileContext>, and reads ctx.context(Position).

Each invoice records the sequence of the order it was made from. Macros Manual examples/file_position_key.rs /// Records each invoice with the sequence of the order it came from, so the next run knows /// where to resume. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), reply)] async fn invoice(order: &Order, Ctx(at): Ctx<Position>) -> Invoiced { tracing::info!(order.id, ?at, "invoiced"); let sequence = match at { FilePosition::Sequence(sequence) => sequence, // A delivery always sits at a sequence; the other forms name places to start or seek to. FilePosition::Beginning | FilePosition::End | FilePosition::Timestamp(_) => 0, }; Invoiced { order: order.id, sequence, } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoicing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss"), |b| { b.include(invoice); }, ) } examples/manual/file_position_key.rs /// Records each invoice with the sequence of the order it came from, so the next run knows /// where to resume. struct Invoice; impl Handle<Order, Invoiced, (), FileContext> for Invoice { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, FileContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Invoiced, HandlerOutcome>> { let at = ctx.context(Position); tracing::info!(order.id, ?at, "invoiced"); let sequence = match at { FilePosition::Sequence(sequence) => sequence, // A delivery always sits at a sequence; the other forms name places to start or // seek to. FilePosition::Beginning | FilePosition::End | FilePosition::Timestamp(_) => 0, }; ready(Ok(Invoiced { order: order.id, sequence, })) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoicing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss"), |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Invoice) .reply() .build(), ); }, ) }

Ctx<SeekHandle> moves the running subscription; what was queued is discarded and a position past the tip is refused. Ctx(seeker): Ctx<SeekHandle> binds a FileSeeker for the subscription the delivery came from (SeekHandle). Its seek(position) takes a FilePosition, and the next delivery comes from there. Deliveries already queued from the old place are discarded. Seek to a position the file has reached. The sequence the file writes next is the tip, and a seek there succeeds. A sequence further ahead, and an instant later than every message the file holds, are refused with an error. A live subscription then ends, and a replay stays where it was. A position read with Ctx<Position>, the beginning and the tip are always within the file. A seek after the broker has shut down returns an error. A batch body reaches the same handle through FileBatchContext. In the manual form the body names FileContext as its context and reads ctx.context(SeekHandle). A position that has to hold across a restart belongs in start_at.

Job 2 says the jobs up to sequence 4 cannot be processed, so the subscription jumps past job 3. Macros Manual examples/file_seek.rs /// Skips a run of jobs known to fail: the subscription jumps to `resume_at`. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("jobs"), start_at(FilePosition::beginning()))] async fn work(job: &Job, Ctx(seeker): Ctx<SeekHandle>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(job.id, "worked"); let Some(resume_at) = job.resume_at else { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); }; if let Err(error) = seeker.seek(FilePosition::sequence(resume_at)).await { tracing::warn!(job.id, resume_at, %error, "seek refused"); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The worker on the job file `main` hands it. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include(work); }) } examples/manual/file_seek.rs /// Skips a run of jobs known to fail: the subscription jumps to `resume_at`. struct Work; impl Handle<Job, (), (), FileContext> for Work { async fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, FileContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { tracing::info!(job.id, "worked"); let Some(resume_at) = job.resume_at else { return Ok(()); }; let seeker = ctx.context(SeekHandle); if let Err(error) = seeker.seek(FilePosition::sequence(resume_at)).await { tracing::warn!(job.id, resume_at, %error, "seek refused"); } Ok(()) } } /// The worker on the job file `main` hands it. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("jobs"), Work) .start_at(FilePosition::beginning()) .build(), ); }) }

start_at opens a subscription at a position on every startup; a stored sequence is how a service resumes on a stream file. It is a clause of the attribute, start_at(FilePosition::beginning()), or .start_at(position) among the mount-site settings. The mount-site form takes a position the service learns only when it starts, such as a stored checkpoint. A subscription with no start_at opens at the tip. The file keeps no record of how far a service read, because ack and nack report Unsupported on this transport (Acknowledgement). So a service that resumes where it stopped stores the sequence it reached, read with Ctx<Position>, and opens the next run at the first sequence it did not handle. FilePosition::sequence(n) delivers message n itself, so the stored sequence of the last handled message is the one to add one to. The sequence the file writes next, one after its last message, opens the subscription at the tip, so a service that handled every message resumes there. A sequence further ahead stops the service at startup. The position applies on every startup: a subscription that starts at the beginning handles the whole retained file each time the service starts. The guide Resuming and seeking builds a service that stores its sequence and resumes there.

The previous run invoiced the orders up to sequence 3, so this run opens at sequence 4. Macros Manual examples/file_start_at.rs /// Invoices each order once, across restarts. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"))] async fn invoice(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "invoiced"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The service, opened at the first sequence the previous run did not invoice. fn app(file: FileBroker, resume_at: u64) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoicing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include(invoice.start_at(FilePosition::sequence(resume_at))); }) } examples/manual/file_start_at.rs /// Invoices each order once, across restarts. struct Invoice; impl Handle<Order> for Invoice { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "invoiced"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The service, opened at the first sequence the previous run did not invoice. fn app(file: FileBroker, resume_at: u64) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoicing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Invoice) .start_at(FilePosition::sequence(resume_at)) .build(), ); }) }

Publish is each form's one policy and its default: replies, slots and lifecycle hooks publish through it with no per-message setting. Each form's prelude names its own policy Publish: FilePublish on a stream file, StdioPublish on a pipe. A service that uses both brokers globs the crate's prelude and writes the two names in full. The policy holds no connection; the runtime pairs it with the connected broker at startup. A registration that names no policy for its reply publishes through Publish, so the bare reply clause needs nothing at the mount site. .out(Ledger, Publish) wires an Out slot, and after_startup(Publish, ..) hands a lifecycle hook a publisher. A reply goes to the stream key its type declares with #[outgoing(name = "receipts")]. A reply type that declares no key is published where the subscriber says, with reply("receipts"). A publish carries a stream key and a payload, and its headers ride inside the payload in an envelope. The policy has no per-message setting, so the publish builder gains no step from this crate and a handler body keeps the plain bound Out<impl Publisher, Marker>. Each publish is written on its own: two publishes of one handler are two separate writes.

The service answers each order with a receipt and writes an audit line through the ledger slot. Macros Manual examples/sea_publish.rs /// The answer to an order, appended under the key the type declares. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order: u64, } /// The audit line of an order, on a key of its own. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "audit")] struct Audited { order: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Audited)] struct Ledger; /// Answers each order with a receipt and writes its audit line through the ledger slot. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), reply)] async fn confirm( order: &Order, Out(ledger): Out<impl Publisher, Ledger>, ) -> Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome> { if let Err(error) = ledger.message(&Audited { order: order.id }).publish().await { tracing::warn!(order.id, %error, "the audit line was not written"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(Receipt { order: order.id }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("checkout", "0.1.0")).with_broker( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss"), |b| { // The reply needs no policy: the runtime pairs the form's own `Publish`. b.include(confirm).out(Ledger, Publish).build(); }, ) } examples/manual/sea_publish.rs /// The answer to an order, appended under the key the type declares. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order: u64, } /// The audit line of an order, on a key of its own. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "audit")] struct Audited { order: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Audited)] struct Ledger; /// Answers each order with a receipt and writes its audit line through the ledger slot. struct Confirm; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, Receipt, Outs<(Entry,)>> for Confirm where Entry: OutEntry<Ledger, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome> { let ledger = outs.get(Ledger); if let Err(error) = ledger.message(&Audited { order: order.id }).publish().await { tracing::warn!(order.id, %error, "the audit line was not written"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(Receipt { order: order.id }) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("checkout", "0.1.0")).with_broker( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss"), |b| { // The reply needs no policy: the runtime pairs the form's own `Publish`. b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Confirm) .reply() .build(), ) .out(Ledger, Publish) .build(); }, ) }

A file publish appends under the destination's stream key and flushes, so a live subscriber or another reader sees it once the call returns. FilePublish, Publish in file::prelude, pairs into a FilePublisher on the file the broker opened. A publish appends the message under its stream key and flushes it to the file, so the bytes have reached the operating system when the call returns. A live subscription of that key reads the message next, and so does another process that reads the same file. The file is synced to the storage device when the broker shuts down. Publishes into one file go one at a time, across every broker of the process opened on that path. A stream key is a place inside the file, so the destination is the key alone and the path is named once, in FileBroker::new. Under size_limit, the publish that reaches the cap fails with SeaFileError::Publish, and every later publish to that file returns that error at once. A publisher kept from before the shutdown returns SeaFileError::NotConnected. A hook registered with after_startup runs once the subscriptions are open, and a hook that returns an error stops the startup.

The service leaves a record under lifecycle each time it starts. Macros Manual examples/file_publish.rs /// The record a service leaves in the file each time it starts. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "lifecycle")] struct Started { service: String, } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss"), |b| { b.include(ship); // Runs once the subscriptions are open; a refused append fails the startup. b.after_startup(Publish, async move |file| { file.message(&Started { service: "shipping".to_owned(), }) .publish() .await }); }, ) } examples/manual/file_publish.rs /// The record a service leaves in the file each time it starts. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "lifecycle")] struct Started { service: String, } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Ship).build()); // Runs once the subscriptions are open; a refused append fails the startup. b.after_startup(Publish, async move |file| { file.message(&Started { service: "shipping".to_owned(), }) .publish() .await }); }, ) }

A stdio publish writes one line to standard output under its stream key; an empty message is refused because a pipe drops empty lines. StdioPublish, Publish in stdio::prelude, pairs into a StdioPublisher. A publish writes one line in the line format, with the message's stream key in its header. The next stage of the pipeline reads that line. This process's own subscriptions do not, because standard output never reaches the same process's standard input; loopback changes that for a test. A payload a text line would change, such as binary data or a payload with a newline, leaves in an envelope and arrives whole (Payloads). A message with no payload and no headers would be an empty line, which the line format drops. So the publisher refuses it with SeaFileError::Invalid, and nothing is written.

The stage answers each word with the same word in capitals, as a line under shouts. Macros Manual examples/stdio_publish.rs /// The line this stage writes for the next one. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "shouts")] struct Shout { text: String, } /// Answers each word with the same word in capitals. #[subscriber("words", reply)] async fn shout(word: &Word) -> Shout { Shout { text: word.text.to_uppercase(), } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shouter", "0.1.0")).with_broker(StdioBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(shout).out_retry(Publish).to("words.retry"); }) } examples/manual/stdio_publish.rs /// The line this stage writes for the next one. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "shouts")] struct Shout { text: String, } /// Answers each word with the same word in capitals. struct ShoutBack; impl Handle<Word, Shout> for ShoutBack { fn handle( &self, word: &Word, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Shout, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Shout { text: word.text.to_uppercase(), })) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shouter", "0.1.0")).with_broker(StdioBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("words", ShoutBack).reply().build()) .out_retry(Publish) .to("words.retry"); }) }

ack and nack report Unsupported on both brokers: nothing records how far a service read, so it resumes from a stored position. A handler settles a delivery as on any broker, with HandlerOutcome::ack or another outcome. The runtime passes the settlement to the transport, which answers AckError::Unsupported, and the runtime logs a warning naming the subscription. A stream file keeps no record of a reader, and the file client's resumable mode is not implemented. So a subscription opens where its descriptor says on every start, whatever the previous run acknowledged. A service that resumes stores the sequence it reached, read with Ctx<Position>, and opens the next run there with start_at. A pipe has no log to go back to: a line read is gone, whatever the handler answers. What a handler asks for beyond ack still happens, because the runtime does it: retry_after on a stream file, out_retry on a pipe, a cap and a dead-letter key on both.

The service invoices every order the file holds; acknowledged orders are read again on the next start. Macros Manual examples/sea_acknowledgement.rs /// Invoices every order the file holds, on every start. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), start_at(FilePosition::beginning()))] async fn invoice(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "invoiced"); // Reported as unsupported: the next start reads this order again. HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The invoicing service on the file `main` hands it. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoicing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include(invoice); }) } examples/manual/sea_acknowledgement.rs /// Invoices every order the file holds, on every start. struct Invoice; impl Handle<Order> for Invoice { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "invoiced"); // Reported as unsupported: the next start reads this order again. ready(Ok(())) } } /// The invoicing service on the file `main` hands it. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoicing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Invoice) .start_at(FilePosition::beginning()) .build(), ); }) }

dead_letter names the stream key a spent delivery is written to, with its payload, its headers and its delivery count. dead_letter(key) goes beside max_attempts(n). The delivery that reaches the cap is published under that key instead of coming back. It keeps its payload and the headers it arrived with, and its retry count says how many deliveries the message got. On a stream file the key is one more stream inside the same file. On a pipe it is a line under that key, which a downstream stage reads. A service reads the dead letters with a subscription of their own, or a replay when an operator inspects them.

A label that fails three times is written under labels.dead. Macros Manual examples/file_dead_letter.rs /// Prints a parcel label; the printer is jammed, so every attempt asks for another. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("labels"))] async fn print(label: &Label) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(label.parcel, "printer jammed"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RETRY_DELAY) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("labels", "0.1.0")).with_broker( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/labels.ss"), |b| { b.include(print) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("labels.dead"); }, ) } examples/manual/file_dead_letter.rs /// Prints a parcel label; the printer is jammed, so every attempt asks for another. struct Print; impl Handle<Label> for Print { fn handle( &self, label: &Label, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(label.parcel, "printer jammed"); ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RETRY_DELAY))) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("labels", "0.1.0")).with_broker( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/labels.ss"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(FileStream::new("labels"), Print).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("labels.dead"); }, ) }

On a pipe a deferred copy goes to the next stage, so the mount site names it with out_retry(Publish).to(key) or the service does not start. out_retry(policy) names the publisher the runtime's deferred copies leave through, and .to(key) names the stream key they go to. Standard output reaches the next process in the pipeline and never this one's standard input. So a copy cannot come back to the stage that deferred it, and the stage says where it goes. Every registration on StdioBroker names it, because a handler may answer retry_after on any delivery. A registration that names none stops the service at startup, with an error that names the subscription and the .to(..) step that fixes it. The copy leaves once the delay is over, and a downstream stage reads it under that key, for example to feed it back to the start of the pipeline. On a stream file the copy needs no destination (retry_after), and out_retry(Publish) there only replaces the publisher. The position is a slot, so .transform(..) runs on the copy; the copy carries the delivery's own bytes, so no codec encodes it.

The stage hands every job it cannot run now to jobs.retry after five seconds.
